topComments.author: chr15m
topComments.text: Will we ever see a soundness bug in the lean kernel again? To a software developer the question seems insane. There were bugs in the past, of course there will be more. When we see those bugs, what will it mean for AI lean proofs? Can we trust them? This whole thing boils down to trust. We can trust human verifications highly because of community and reputation and human proof-of-work. Humans sometimes lie about math results but it's rare because of this. They make mistakes and those mistakes are discovered by communities who are themselves largely trustworthy because of this. LLMs don't care about reputation. They hallucinate and fabricate often. In harnesses they literally try to cheat and bend rules, which is a disaster for knowledge that is encoded in rules. So we have to rely on proof checkers. The problem is, how trustworthy are proof checkers? Are there bugs? And is the underlying theory itself free of paradoxes and unknowables and mathematical "bugs" that can be exploited? Imagine a human mathematician hell bent on deceiving other mathematicians - would we trust their breakthroughs, even with a verifier? Because of these properties, the final backstop has to be humans, and rooted in the community and proof-of-work based human trust system. At the moment people are trusting the tools too much. Prediction: bugs will be found by humans using AI tools that call into question the Navier-Stokes proof.

The only thing that makes these people happy is zero data retention and deterministic redaction at the source. Regex over arbitrary string literals does not represent determinism in this context. If your product is handling natural language conversations from end customers, there is not much you can do to prevent the occasional PII leak without ruining the rest of the pie. ZDR is your best mitigation if you actually want the magical AI experience to work the way the investors hope it can. PII can often become disclosed by way of many correlated factors that are not considered PII on their own. Even a perfect AI system cannot capture all of these relationships. You could probably locate where I live within a 20 mile radius if you spent enough time analyzing my HN comments over the years. Not one of these comments on their own would trigger a PII filter.

jobs.text: I’m Chris, VP Engineering at Fazeshift. We’re nine engineers plus our Founder/CTO and me, and I’m hiring someone who can help us do more, better: increase both what we can build and the quality and sophistication of the software we build. Accounts receivable sounds boring until you look under the hood. It sits at the intersection of money, business relationships, software systems of various vintages, and a huge amount of repetitive human work. Instead of giving finance teams another dashboard to stare at, we’re building AI agents that actually do the work across billing, collections, payments, cash application, and the systems connecting them. We’ve grown revenue 12x since 2024, and eight unicorns now run AR on Fazeshift. A big part of what makes the engineering interesting is that we’re intentionally not the system of record. Our customers already run on ERPs, CRMs, banks, billing systems, payment processors, spreadsheets, and internal software, so we have to understand state across systems we don’t control, act safely in them, and recover when reality disagrees with what an API says should have happened. A timeout doesn’t necessarily mean a write failed. Webhooks can arrive late or twice. A payment may not contain enough information to identify an invoice. In those cases, blindly retrying can be exactly the wrong thing to do. We use coding agents heavily ourselves. Engineers use Conductor, stacked PRs, Linear, and multiple frontier models every day, with internal skills and tooling that let agents drive and validate our local development environment. We’re especially interested in engineers whose development workflow has already materially changed because of coding agents: people who are comfortable delegating meaningful work, keeping independent threads moving in parallel, debugging where agents get stuck, and improving the surrounding system when the workflow breaks down. But generated code is still your code . Judgment, debugging, systems thinking, taste, and understanding what actually shipped matter more here, not less. Our development style is roughly: design enough to find the shape of the problem, then build to learn. There’s a short distance here between noticing a problem, deciding what should happen, building it, and seeing the result in production with our customers. You’ll own meaningful problems from ambiguity through design, implementation, rollout, and production, and you’ll work directly with the people affected by what you build. We’re looking for 5+ years of professional experience, strong TypeScript/full-stack skills, solid systems judgment, and real production ownership. No fintech background needed. What I'm looking for is a way to detect gamepad button presses as an event listener rather than polling since that would be more accurate. Is there a way to do that?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Why do POSIX and the C FAQ suggest casting char ** to const char * const *?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: It is established in ISO/IEC 9899:2018 that an implicit assignment of a char ** (such as the address of a char * ) to a const char ** is unsafe, and its reasoning is explicitly illustrated in §6.5.16.2, p. 74, ¶6: EXAMPLE 3 Consider the fragment: const char **cpp; char *p; const char c = 'A'; cpp = &p; // constraint violation *cpp = &c; // valid *p = 0; // valid The first assignment is unsafe because it would allow the following valid code to attempt to change the value of the const object c. Furthermore, in Volume 2 (System Interfaces) of POSIX.1-2024 on p. 875, ¶29858 within the rationale for the exec family of functions, the authors express regret regarding this limitation and note that an explicit cast would be required as a workaround: Specifying two levels of const−qualification for the argv[ ] and envp[ ] parameters for the exec functions may seem to be the natural choice. [...] Instead, only the array of pointers is noted as constant. [...] The only other possibility is the fourth column, but using it would require a cast on the argv or envp arguments. Similarly, although it lacks normative authority, the comp.lang.c FAQ (Summit, Question 11.10) references the use of such a cast: In C, if you must assign or pass pointers which have qualifier mismatches at other than the first level of indirection, you must use explicit casts (e.g. ( const char ** ) in this case), although as always, the need for such a cast may indicate a deeper problem which the cast doesn't really fix. stackOverflowQuestions.title: Why does the GCC compiler generate operands and mnemonics that specify just the low-order bytes instead of using the declared size?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm just reading the book Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective , and in an example from Section 3.5.3, it shows us the different operations along with their assembly counterpart. Example: C code: long arith(long x, long y, long z){ long t1 = x ^ y; long t2 = z * 48; long t3 = t1 & 0x0F0F0F0F; long t4 = t2 - t3; return t4; } Assembly code: xorq %rsi, %rdi leaq (%rdx,%rdx,2), %rax salq $4, %rax andl $252645135, %edi subq %rdi, %rax ret Questions: Wouldn't the GCC compiler be expected to use the %rdi register for the and operation, as shown above? Since, we are working with a long , which is a quad word. If we use the 32-bit %edi register instead, aren't we simply discarding the upper 32 bits of %rdi ? Would this affect the result if the numeric value is larger than 32 bits? What rules or policies does GCC follow when deciding which register size to use? Extra: Why transform the hexadecimal value to decimal, or is it just the human-readable output format? I got the assembly code by using gcc -Og -S example.c with GCC 13.3.0

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare Traces Turns the Proxy Layer into OpenTelemetry Spans, with New Volume-Based Pricing
infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare has put Traces into open beta, extending automatic tracing from Workers to security rules, transformations, cache, routing and origin handling as OpenTelemetry spans. Traces accept and forward W3C traceparent headers, and Trace Rules allow targeted sampling. Pricing moves to ingestion and retention volume from December 1. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Android Bench 2 Adds Support for Long-Horizon Tasks, Agentic Evaluation, and Continuous Scoring
infoqArticles.description: Google has released Android Bench 2.0, a major update to its benchmark framework for evaluating AI models and agents on Android development tasks. The update introduces long-horizon tasks (LHTs), agent-based evaluation, and continuous scoring to better assess performance on complex, multi-step development tasks. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Shopify Upgrades Checkout Blocks to Polaris Web Components, Cutting Bundle Sizes up to 85%
infoqArticles.description: Shopify has updated its Checkout Blocks app, transitioning five high-traffic checkout UI extensions to remote-dom using Preact and Polaris web components. The rewrite, which involved moving to TypeScript and a new API version, led to significant reductions in bundle sizes and load times. From October 1, 2026, only the updated versions will be supported. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Github Migrates Copilot Runtime to Rust with AI-Assisted Rewrite
infoqArticles.description: GitHub migrated more than 800,000 lines of Copilot runtime code from TypeScript and Node.js to Rust in about 14.5 weeks using AI-assisted development. The incremental migration used N-API interoperability, automated testing, human review, and 128 pull requests while continuing to ship releases. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: CircleCI Makes Machine Runner Orchestrator Generally Available

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Ontology‐Driven Observability: Building the E2E Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
infoqArticles.description: Prasanna Vijayanathan and Renzo Sanchez-Silva share how Netflix tackles observability across 38M events/sec. They discuss replacing reactive monitoring with an AI-driven operational ontology and agentic workflows using Claude and graph databases. They explain how unifying MELT telemetry into queryable knowledge graphs enables automated triaging, root-cause analysis, and self-healing systems. By Pr
infoqArticles.author: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva

infoqArticles.title: Olson and Söderqvist Discuss Valkey’s Evolution and Future Past Caching Use Cases at OSS EU
infoqArticles.description: Valkey is a growing project, launched as a fork of Redis over two years ago, supported by twelve maintainers and nine committee members from various companies. The project also emphasises security and release efficiency through automation. By Olim

infoqArticles.author: Claudio Masolo

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare K2 Builds Event Streams on R2 Object Storage, at a Second of Produce Latency
infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare has launched K2 in public beta, a serverless event streaming service implementing a durable log on R2 object storage. Cloudflare states produce latency of about one second at p99; a tester reported end-to-end p99 of 7.5 seconds, which a commenter answering for the team said was higher than expected. Consume charges match produce charges per GB. By Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Multi-Agent Patterns from Spotify’s AI Powered Advertising Platform
infoqArticles.description: Pratik Rasam discusses how Spotify Ads Manager runs production-grade multi-agent systems at scale using Google ADK Java. He shares key architectural patterns, domain ownership models, deterministic guardrails, and tracing-based evaluation strategies, detailing hard-learned lessons on drawing agent boundaries, optimizing tool schemas, and managing costs while avoiding monolithic agent pitfalls. By
infoqArticles.author: Pratik Rasam
